entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Burgundofara (c. 595 – April 3, 656), known posthumously as Saint Fara or Fare, was a pivotal figure in the development of early medieval monasticism in Francia, establishing the influential Abbey of Faremoutiers in the early 7th century. Born into the powerful Austrasian aristocracy as the daughter of Count Agneric and Leudegundis, she defied societal expectations by dedicating her life to religious devotion rather than a politically advantageous marriage. Her foundation, initially a double monastery for men and women, became a beacon of spiritual and intellectual life under the Merovingian dynasty, deeply influencing female monasticism across Gaul.

Inspired by the Irish missionary Columbanus, who visited her family's estate in Brie around 610, Burgundofara chose a monastic path, reportedly receiving the veil from him. Despite initial resistance from her father, who wished her to marry, she persevered, eventually securing the patronage of King Dagobert I and his queen, Nanthild. Around 627, she founded the Abbey of Faremoutiers (Latin: Monasterium Scotorum, 'Monastery of the Scots'), named for its adherence to the Rule of Saint Columbanus and later incorporating elements of the Benedictine Rule. As its first abbess for nearly three decades until her death, she oversaw its growth into a prominent spiritual center, attracting noblewomen and fostering a unique blend of Irish and Roman monastic traditions.
